prize_parts.citation: For the design of ionizable lipid nanoparticles that enable the delivery of nucleic-acid medicines

statement.case_for: After reading the openings I move B016 to first place. It is lipid self-assembly put to work: the pH-dependent charge of an ionizable lipid, its bilayer-to-non-bilayer phase behaviour, and the way these govern encapsulation of nucleic acid and endosomal release are physical-chemical principles that were worked out and then converted into medicines (siRNA therapy and mRNA vaccines). Four members place it in their top three or seven (Aili first, Chabes third, Aqvist seventh, myself second), and it is the most clinically validated item on the shortlist. The Vancouver work of Cullis, Hope and Madden on entrapment, ionizable lipids and formulation is the molecular foundation on which the later siRNA and mRNA products were built, and a trio drawn from that core is the most defensible reading of the credit.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution and category. Credit is genuinely spread over the Vancouver group, MacLachlan and the industrial SNALP development, and Anderson and Langer with their lipidoid libraries, so a three-person limit leaves out real contributors. A second concern is whether this is perceived as chemistry or as pharmaceutical formulation, and whether the 2023 Medicine prize for nucleoside-modified mRNA already covers much of the public story. B003, my own earlier first choice, is conceptually the most appealing to me as a physical chemist, but the in vivo relevance debate is not settled, and I should not let disciplinary affinity outweigh maturity.

responses.point: B016 should be ranked first because ionizable lipid nanoparticles turned fragile nucleic acids into deployable drugs, and he would favour Cullis, Anderson and MacLachlan.
responses.response: I agree on the ranking and on the importance of pKa-tuned design and self-assembly. I differ on the trio: lipidoid combinatorial libraries are a distinct screening strategy that came later, whereas the ionizable-lipid concept, entrapment and bilayer physical chemistry came from Cullis, Hope and Madden. If the committee wants the lipidoid and clinical translation strands represented, we should discuss that explicitly rather than assume Anderson belongs by default, and I could move to Anderson in place of Hope if the evidence on priority supports it.

responses.point: B003 is attractive to a physicist but is still contested: physiological relevance of condensates is debated and much evidence depends on overexpression, so it may be premature. His first place is B067 nanopore sequencing, resting on a clean physical principle.
responses.response: I accept his maturity objection on B003 and have lowered it for that reason, even though it was my own first choice. On B067, I find the physical principle elegant, but the committee would face a real allocation problem among Branton, Deamer, Bayley, Kasianowicz and Akeson, and the decisive step of base discrimination came from engineered pores and enzyme control. I would like him to say which three he would credit and why, because this is where I think B067 is vulnerable compared with B016, whose core group is clearer.

responses.point: B009 is a genuinely new pharmacological modality, a game-changer, but timing may be slightly early since no degrader is widely approved. He ranks B016 seventh because of overlap with the Medicine prize.
responses.response: I respect the novelty of induced proximity and have it as an alternative. My concern is the same as his: clinical proof is still arriving and the credit splits into PROTAC and molecular glue strands. On overlap, I do not think the Medicine prize closes the door for B016: that prize recognised nucleoside modification of the RNA, while the delivery vehicle is a separate molecular-design problem that the vaccines could not have reached patients without. A chemistry prize here would honour a different achievement, which I think is an important distinction.

responses.point: B027 long-range electron transfer through proteins is a mechanistic foundation for bioenergetics, with Gray and Winkler as a clean two-person credit, confirmed over decades.
responses.response: The attribution is indeed cleaner than in most candidates, and as a physical chemist I value the distance and driving-force relations. My reservation is impact and timing: the field is textbook, and the Marcus-theory prize of 1992 already recognised the underlying electron-transfer framework, so I would ask whether the protein-specific extension is large enough to stand alone as a prize at this stage compared with the broad consequences of B016.

uncertainties: Fair allocation among Cullis, Hope, Madden, MacLachlan, Anderson and Langer, and whether the lipidoid strand deserves a place.
Whether the committee regards ionizable lipid nanoparticles as chemistry rather than formulation, given the 2023 Medicine prize.
Whether the in vivo functional relevance of condensates (B003) will be settled enough to treat it as mature.
Priority questions between the academic ionizable-lipid work and industrial SNALP development.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile: none of the B016 candidates is connected to Lund or to my own research group. I share Lund affiliation with Heiner Linke and Peter Somfai, and my lipid and membrane work is scientifically adjacent to B016 and B003, but that is a matter of expertise and not a recusal issue.
